rejected_videos.reason: Technical-accuracy hard rejection: at 422 seconds the speaker states, "A p-value is literally the false positive probability." A p-value is not the experiment's false-positive probability; it is a null-conditional probability of results at least as extreme as those observed. Although the following captions give that conditional definition, the explicit misidentification risks teaching an incorrect interpretation central to f4. The introductory button-color example at 140–198 seconds offers partial coverage, but does not explain why random assignment reduces preexisting group differences or cover the required planning and interpretation facts. Later material concentrates on advanced sequential testing rather than a standalone beginner-to-job-ready lesson, and does not supply the complete traffic, baseline-performance, and duration-planning guidance required by f5–f6.

Reject for technical inaccuracies, not merely missing coverage. At 29–36s, the video describes statistical significance as being 90–95 percent sure that repeating the test will give the same results; significance does not establish that replication probability. At 54–69s, it treats an inconclusive result as showing neither variant is better and providing no information, rather than insufficient evidence to establish improvement under the chosen threshold. The calculator demo begins at 75s but relies on the preceding misleading explanation and does not explain its significance threshold or assumptions. No clean standalone range adequately corrects these problems. The video also omits random assignment, pre-exposure experiment planning, and prospective sample-size/duration estimation.

No clean, prerequisite-safe standalone segment meets the required teaching objective. At 79–83 seconds, the worked example concludes that version B is better solely because it generated more sales leads, without establishing statistical significance under a chosen threshold. This contradicts f4, rather than merely omitting it. The subsequent sampling and random-chance caveats do not retract that conclusion or explain how to interpret Not Significant or Inconclusive results. Trimming away the conclusion would leave the example unfinished; starting with the sampling discussion would require the earlier example. The video also omits the complete pre-exposure plan required by f3 and the feasibility inputs and advance sample/duration estimation required by f5–f6. Later sections rely on machine-learning deployment knowledge not taught on this path or return to earlier examples.

No clean, prerequisite-safe standalone range adequately covers the intended facts. The introduction moves into blocked Data-Driven Decision Making at 25 seconds. The potentially useful example beginning at 58 seconds explains variant changes and predeclared success criteria, but its sample-size explanation runs directly into an untaught multivariate/full-factorial example at 118–131 seconds; ending at 118 would leave the preceding sentence unfinished. Later material introduces machine-learning recommendations and A/A testing without establishing their prerequisites. Coverage gaps, rather than explicit factual contradictions, also remain: random assignment's role in reducing preexisting group differences is not explained; target audience and planned run conditions are not fully specified; significance is mentioned without the chosen-threshold and inconclusive-result interpretation required by f4; and traffic, baseline performance, minimum detectable effect, and pre-build duration estimation required by f5–f6 are absent.

No clean standalone segment serves this path's staged-rollout objective. The opening examples (0–334s) depend on untaught engineering details, including database migration, configuration objects, and application branching. The definition section begins mid-transition at 334s and refers back to those examples. It explains deployment-independent behavior changes and briefly mentions percentage exposure at 403–421s, but never develops an eligible audience, initial exposure, monitored results, or readiness-gated expansion. No section teaches explicit exposure stages with success-metric and feedback checks or an error-log trigger for switching the flag off until fixed (f3 and f5). Rollback is discussed, but the later implementation section relies on untaught caching, latency, and infrastructure concepts rather than providing a Product Manager rollout demonstration. These are coverage and prerequisite gaps, not an identified factual contradiction.

The video gives technically misleading sample-size guidance at 65–72 seconds: “A holdout of a few dozen tells you nothing” and “So wait until each group has” / “hundreds”. There is no universal hundreds-per-group threshold; holdout sizing must reflect available traffic and the statistical needs of the comparison (f4). Trimming before this advice leaves a useful definition and illustrative incremental-effect calculation, but not the required sizing or consistent-assignment guidance. The later section emphasizes ending and rerunning a short test rather than maintaining a baseline to measure long-run impact, and does not explicitly establish consistent assignment and exclusions throughout the observation period (f5). No clean range adequately serves the intended lesson.

No clean standalone segment serves the intended readiness assessment. The video explains organizational capabilities, partially supporting f1, but does not cover technical quality, monitoring, operational response, evidence and owners for checks, unresolved actions, or a justified proceed/hold recommendation (f2–f4). Its checklist example introduces sales-team capabilities at timestamp 153 and develops sales qualification and prospect progression, overlapping blocked Sales & Support Enablement content. Ending at 153 would also cut the preceding fact-bearing sentence, whose completion shares that caption with the example transition. The brief opening definition is prerequisite-safe but is not a sufficient assessment mini-lesson. These are coverage and prerequisite-safety problems, not an identified factual contradiction.

No clean segment teaches the intended product-launch enablement objective. The video focuses on buyer-facing marketing content, pre-call reading, and sales content libraries rather than preparing sales and support teams to explain and support a new product. It provides limited overlap with practical sales materials (f2), but does not teach a team-specific enablement plan with training, owners, and completion timing (f3), a pre-launch readiness check (f4), or an enablement packet containing value, talking points, FAQs, known limitations, and escalation routes (f5). Support enablement is absent. This is a scope and coverage mismatch, not an identified factual contradiction.

No standalone range teaches the intended objective: translating usability findings into concrete design decisions. Recording and sharing observations provide partial supporting workflow only; no worked findings table or completed synthesis example is present.
